choices.text: A 1,2-halo alcohol, with a halogen and an −OH on neighboring carbons
A 1,2-dihalide, with a halogen on each of two neighboring carbons
choices.why: That is the product of X2 addition without water. A halohydrin has one halogen and one −OH.

choices.text: An alcohol made by adding H2O across a double bond
choices.why: That is just an alcohol. A halohydrin also contains a halogen.

choices.text: A compound with a halogen and an −OH on the same carbon
choices.why: The halogen and −OH are on adjacent carbons: it's a 1,2-halo alcohol.

explanation: Reaction of an alkene with Br2 or Cl2 in the presence of water gives a 1,2-halo alcohol, called a halohydrin. The net effect is addition of HO–X across the double bond.

prompt: In bromohydrin formation, what role does water play?

choices.text: It acts as a nucleophile, competing with Br− to react with the bromonium ion
It protonates the alkene to form a carbocation that Br− then attacks
choices.why: The first step is formation of a bromonium ion from Br2. Water then attacks that ion as a nucleophile.

choices.text: It acts as the electrophile that adds to the alkene before Br2 does
choices.why: Br2 supplies the electrophile. Water, with its lone pairs, is the nucleophile.

choices.text: It only dissolves the reactants and doesn't take part in the reaction
choices.why: Water ends up in the product as the −OH group.

explanation: With Br2 alone, the bromonium ion reacts with the only nucleophile present, Br−. With a high concentration of water, water competes with Br− and reacts with the bromonium ion; loss of a proton then gives the bromohydrin.

prompt: In bromohydrin formation, how many of the two bromine atoms of each Br2 molecule end up bonded to carbon in the organic product?
explanation: One bromine becomes part of the bromonium ion and stays on carbon; the other leaves as Br−. Water, not Br−, then attacks, so the net effect is addition of HO–Br: one Br and one OH.

prompt: What is the organic product when 2-butene, CH3CH=CHCH3, reacts with Br2 in the presence of water?

choices.text: 3-Bromo-2-butanol
2,3-Dibromobutane
choices.why: That is the product without water. In water, water competes with Br− as the nucleophile.

choices.text: 2-Butanol
choices.why: The product keeps a bromine on the carbon next to the −OH.

choices.text: 2-Bromobutane
choices.why: That would come from HBr addition. The bromohydrin also has an −OH group.

explanation: Br2 forms a bromonium ion, water attacks it, and loss of a proton gives the bromohydrin, with Br on one former double-bond carbon and OH on the other: 3-bromo-2-butanol, along with H3O+.

prompt: Why is N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) often used for bromohydrin formation instead of Br2?

choices.text: It is a stable, easily handled source that releases Br2 slowly at a controlled rate
It adds −OH directly to the alkene without forming a bromonium ion
choices.why: NBS is just a source of Br2; the reaction still goes through a bromonium ion.

choices.text: It makes alkenes soluble in pure water so that no other solvent is needed
choices.why: Few alkenes are soluble in water, which is why a solvent such as aqueous DMSO is used.

choices.text: It brominates aromatic rings as well as the alkene double bond
choices.why: In the section's styrene example, the aromatic ring does not react.

explanation: Few alkenes are soluble in water, so bromohydrin formation is often run in aqueous DMSO using NBS as a source of Br2. NBS is stable and easily handled, and it decomposes slowly in water to give Br2 at a controlled rate. Br2 itself can be used but is more dangerous and harder to handle.

prompt: What is the product when styrene, C6H5CH=CH2, reacts with NBS in aqueous DMSO?

choices.text: 2-Bromo-1-phenylethanol, C6H5CH(OH)CH2Br
2-Bromo-2-phenylethanol, C6H5CHBrCH2OH
choices.why: The bromine goes to the less substituted CH2 carbon and the −OH to the carbon bearing the ring.

choices.text: 1,2-Dibromo-1-phenylethane, C6H5CHBrCH2Br
choices.why: With water present, water rather than Br− attacks the bromonium ion.

choices.text: A bromohydrin with an extra Br added to the aromatic ring
choices.why: The aromatic ring doesn't react with Br2, even though it appears to have three double bonds.

explanation: NBS supplies Br2, which forms a bromonium ion with the C=C bond. Water ends up on the ring-bearing carbon and Br on the CH2, giving 2-bromo-1-phenylethanol in 70% yield. The aromatic ring is untouched.

prompt: In the section's example, what percent yield of 2-bromo-1-phenylethanol is obtained from styrene with NBS in aqueous DMSO?
explanation: Styrene reacts with NBS and water in DMSO to give 2-bromo-1-phenylethanol in 70% yield. The aromatic ring does not react.

prompt: When styrene reacts with NBS and water, why doesn't its aromatic ring react with Br2?

choices.text: Aromatic rings are unusually stable and less reactive than they appear
The aromatic ring has no carbon–carbon double bonds at all
choices.why: It appears to have three C=C bonds. It doesn't react because aromatic rings are unusually stable.

choices.text: NBS reacts only with double bonds at the very end of a carbon chain
choices.why: NBS is simply a source of Br2; cyclopentene, with no terminal double bond, also reacts.

choices.text: Water protects the ring by forming hydrogen bonds to its π electrons
choices.why: The reason given is the stability of aromatic rings, not any effect of water.

explanation: The aromatic ring of styrene appears to have three carbon–carbon double bonds, yet it doesn't react with Br2. Aromatic rings are a good deal more stable and less reactive than might be expected, a point the book returns to in its chapter on benzene.

prompt: What product would you expect from the reaction of cyclopentene with NBS and water?

choices.text: trans-2-Bromocyclopentanol
cis-2-Bromocyclopentanol
choices.why: Water attacks the bromonium ion from the face opposite the bromine, so Br and OH end up trans.

choices.text: trans-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane
choices.why: That forms without water. Here water is the nucleophile, so the product has an −OH.

choices.text: 1-Bromocyclopentanol
choices.why: Br and OH add to different carbons of the double bond, giving a 1,2-halo alcohol.

explanation: NBS gives Br2, which forms a bromonium ion. Water attacks from the opposite, unshielded face, just as Br− does in bromination, so the bromine and hydroxyl end up trans: trans-2-bromocyclopentanol.

prompt: What is the major product when propene, CH3CH=CH2, is treated with NBS in aqueous DMSO?

choices.text: 1-Bromo-2-propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH2Br
2-Bromo-1-propanol, CH3CHBrCH2OH
choices.why: This puts bromine on the more substituted carbon. In the major product, Br is on the less substituted carbon.

choices.text: 1,2-Dibromopropane, CH3CHBrCH2Br
choices.why: In aqueous DMSO, water attacks the bromonium ion, so the product has an −OH.

choices.text: 2-Propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3
choices.why: The product still contains bromine.

explanation: The major product has the bromine on the less highly substituted carbon (the CH2) and the −OH on the more substituted carbon: CH3CH(OH)CH2Br, 1-bromo-2-propanol.

prompt: In bromohydrin formation from propene, Br bonds to the less substituted carbon and −OH to the more substituted carbon. Which orientation is this?

choices.text: Markovnikov, because the electrophile (Br) goes where H goes in HX addition
Non-Markovnikov, because bromine is on the less substituted carbon
choices.why: Here Br is the electrophile, playing the role of H in HX addition. The nucleophile (−OH) goes to the more substituted carbon, so this is Markovnikov.

choices.text: Neither, because Markovnikov's rule can only describe HX additions
choices.why: The book classifies this result as Markovnikov orientation, judged by where the electrophile and nucleophile end up.

choices.text: Non-Markovnikov, because water is a weaker nucleophile than Br−
choices.why: Orientation depends on where the groups end up. The nucleophile is on the more substituted carbon, which is Markovnikov.

explanation: In HX addition the electrophile H+ goes to the less substituted carbon and the nucleophile X− to the more substituted one. In bromohydrin formation Br is the electrophile and water the nucleophile, so Br on the less substituted carbon and OH on the more substituted carbon is Markovnikov orientation.

prompt: What product would you expect when cyclohexene is treated with Cl2 in the presence of water?

choices.text: trans-2-Chlorocyclohexanol
cis-2-Chlorocyclohexanol
choices.why: Water attacks the chloronium ion from the face opposite the chlorine, giving the trans product.

choices.text: trans-1,2-Dichlorocyclohexane
choices.why: With a high concentration of water, water rather than Cl− attacks the intermediate.

choices.text: Cyclohexanol
choices.why: The chlorine stays in the product; the net addition is HO–Cl.

explanation: Cl2 in water also gives halohydrins. A chloronium ion forms, water attacks it from the opposite face, and loss of a proton gives trans-2-chlorocyclohexanol.

prompt: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, reacts with NBS in aqueous DMSO?

choices.text: 1-Bromo-2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)2C(OH)CH2Br
2-Bromo-2-methyl-1-propanol, (CH3)2CBrCH2OH
choices.why: That puts Br on the more substituted carbon, the reverse of the observed orientation.

choices.text: 1,2-Dibromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)2CBrCH2Br
choices.why: That is the product without water. Here water attacks the bromonium ion.

choices.text: 2-Methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)3COH
choices.why: The product keeps a bromine on the CH2 carbon.

explanation: As with propene, Br bonds to the less substituted carbon (the CH2) and −OH to the more substituted carbon: (CH3)2C(OH)CH2Br, 1-bromo-2-methyl-2-propanol.

prompt: Halohydrins form in marine organisms through haloperoxidase enzymes. In the section's example, what does the bromoperoxidase use along with the alkene?

choices.text: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, and bromide ion, Br−
N-Bromosuccinimide in aqueous DMSO
choices.why: NBS in aqueous DMSO is the laboratory method, not the enzyme's.

choices.text: Bromine, Br2, dissolved in liquid SO2
choices.why: Liquid SO2 isn't involved. The enzyme uses H2O2 to oxidize bromide ion.

choices.text: Hydrogen bromide, HBr, with a strong acid catalyst
choices.why: HBr addition would give an alkyl bromide. The enzyme uses H2O2 and Br−.

explanation: As with halogenation, halohydrin formation in nature is carried out by haloperoxidases. In the section's example, a bromoperoxidase uses H2O2 and Br− (at pH 3) to convert an alkene into a halohydrin.

prompt: After water attacks the bromonium ion, what final step gives the neutral bromohydrin?

choices.text: Loss of a proton, H+, to water, forming H3O+
Loss of Br− from the carbon it is bonded to
choices.why: The bromine stays in the product; it is H+ that is lost.

choices.text: Addition of a second bromine atom to carbon
choices.why: Only one Br ends up in the product; the other Br of Br2 leaves as Br−.

choices.text: Protonation of the oxygen by a molecule of H3O+
choices.why: After water attacks, the oxygen already carries an extra proton. It must lose one, not gain one.

explanation: In the mechanism, Br2 forms the bromonium ion (step 1), water attacks it as a nucleophile (step 2), and the oxygen, now carrying an extra H, loses a proton to water (step 3). With 2-butene, this gives 3-bromo-2-butanol and H3O+.
